triage.name: COPD
triage.reason: Common chronic respiratory disease with classic smoking history, exam findings, and spirometry-confirmed diagnosis.

review_issues: presentation: term 'Sputum production' not found in SNOMED CT
presentation: term 'Sputum production' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Use of accessory muscles' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Prolonged expiratory phase' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Decreased movement of diaphragm' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: Historically more common in men, but prevalence is now similar or higher in women in the United States
More common with lower socioeconomic status

risk_factors.text: Occupational exposure to dusts, fumes, or chemicals
Indoor air pollution from biomass fuel

family_history: COPD in a parent or sibling

chief_complaints.text: I get short of breath doing things that used to be easy
I've had a cough for months
I cough up phlegm most mornings

hpi.onset: Gradual over years, often unnoticed at first
hpi.duration: Chronic, present for months to years before diagnosis
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive; symptoms may start with mild exertional dyspnea and morning cough, then worsen over time with occasional acute exacerbations
hpi.quality: Breathlessness with a sense of tightness or heaviness in the chest
hpi.severity: Variable; often mild initially, moderate to severe by the time of diagnosis
hpi.timing: Worse with exertion, cold air, inhaled irritants, and respiratory infections; cough often worst in the morning
pertinent_negatives: Acute chest pain that worsens with breathing
Coughing up large amounts of blood

argues_against: Acute chest pain radiating to arm or jaw

atypical.how_it_differs: May attribute dyspnea to aging or deconditioning; may present with only fatigue, recurrent infections, or confusion during exacerbations.
Dyspnea may be blamed on weight or deconditioning; wheezing and cough may be less prominent.

general.mild: Comfortable at rest; may have a mild cough
general.moderate: Dyspneic with exertion; may breathe with pursed lips
general.severe: Dyspneic at rest, sitting upright or leaning forward, using accessory muscles
general.critical: In severe respiratory distress, cyanotic, unable to speak in full sentences

findings.maneuver: Inspect the chest for increased anteroposterior diameter
findings.finding: Barrel-shaped chest with increased anterior-posterior diameter

findings.maneuver: Inspect the neck and chest during breathing
findings.finding: Use of accessory muscles of respiration
Cyanosis of lips or nail beds
Wheezing on auscultation, especially on forced expiration
Coarse rhonchi that clear with cough

findings.maneuver: Percuss during deep inspiration and expiration to measure diaphragmatic excursion
Inspect the neck veins with the patient at 45 degrees

labs.caveat: Secondary polycythemia from chronic hypoxemia; not present in all patients.
Metabolic compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis; elevated bicarbonate suggests chronic CO2 retention.
Chronic hypercapnia in advanced COPD; acute worsening may raise PaCO2 further.
Hypoxemia is common with significant obstruction; may be normal in mild disease.
Usually normal in stable COPD due to renal compensation; acidemia indicates acute or acute-on-chronic respiratory failure.

findings.finding: Peaked P waves (P pulmonale) from right atrial enlargement
Right ventricular hypertrophy (dominant R in V1, deep S in V5-V6)
Low QRS voltage in limb leads
Multifocal atrial tachycardia (three or more P wave morphologies, irregular rhythm)

imaging.preferred_when: First-line imaging for chronic dyspnea and suspected COPD

findings.text: Increased retrosternal air space on lateral view
Enlarged central pulmonary arteries or right heart border (cor pulmonale)

imaging.preferred_when: Assessing emphysema extent, lung cancer screening, or when X-ray is inconclusive
Suspected pulmonary hypertension or cor pulmonale

initial.why: Check for secondary polycythemia and anemia that may worsen dyspnea
Assess bicarbonate as a clue to chronic CO2 retention and check renal function before medications
Evaluate for hyperinflation and exclude other causes of dyspnea

supporting.why: Assess oxygenation, ventilation, and acid-base status
supporting.only_if: oxygen saturation <92%, severe disease, or suspected acute respiratory failure

supporting.why: Assess emphysema pattern and exclude bronchiectasis or other pathology
supporting.only_if: suspected alternative diagnosis, lung cancer screening, or planning for lung volume reduction
young patient (<45), minimal smoking, family history of emphysema/COPD, or emphysema predominantly in lower lobes

supporting.why: Evaluate for pulmonary hypertension and right heart strain
supporting.only_if: clinical signs of cor pulmonale (edema, loud P2, JVD, hypoxemia)

not_indicated.why: Not useful for chronic dyspnea unless pulmonary embolism is suspected
Not routine for COPD; consider if heart failure is a likely alternative cause of dyspnea
Not needed for stable COPD; may be used during exacerbations with purulent sputum
not_indicated.only_if: acute exacerbation with suspected bacterial infection

not_indicated.why: Not routinely needed for COPD diagnosis; may be done if cardiac disease is suspected
not_indicated.only_if: chest pain, palpitations, or signs of cor pulmonale

decision_points: Spirometry must be performed after administration of a short-acting bronchodilator to assess reversibility and confirm persistent obstruction.
Arterial blood gas is indicated if oxygen saturation is <92% or if the patient has signs of respiratory failure.
Consider alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in never-smokers, young patients, or those with lower-lobe emphysema.
Chest imaging is used to exclude other causes of dyspnea, not to diagnose COPD itself.

criteria.name: GOLD criteria for COPD diagnosis (paraphrased)
criteria.summary: Confirmation of persistent airflow limitation by spirometry in a patient with appropriate symptoms and exposure history.
items: Symptoms such as dyspnea, chronic cough, or sputum production
History of exposure to tobacco smoke or other lung irritants
No alternative explanation for the airflow obstruction

differential.name: Asthma
differential.why_considered: Episodic wheezing, dyspnea, and cough with partial reversibility can mimic COPD, especially in older adults.

history: Childhood onset or personal/family history of atopy
Episodic symptoms triggered by allergens, exercise, or cold air
Symptoms vary over time and may be absent between attacks
exam: Wheezing on auscultation that resolves between episodes
labs: Spirometry shows significant bronchodilator reversibility (FEV1 increase >12% and >200 mL)
Elevated blood eosinophils or total IgE in allergic asthma
imaging: Chest X-ray usually normal or hyperinflation during exacerbation

differential.name: Heart failure
differential.why_considered: Exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, and fatigue are common in both conditions, especially in older patients with smoking history.
differential.trigger: Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or bilateral crackles in a patient with dyspnea.

history: History of ischemic heart disease, hypertension, or cardiomyopathy
imaging: Cardiomegaly and pulmonary vascular congestion on chest X-ray
Echocardiogram shows reduced ejection fraction or diastolic dysfunction
ecg: Left ventricular hypertrophy, prior myocardial infarction, or atrial fibrillation

differential.name: Pulmonary embolism
differential.why_considered: Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and hypoxemia can occur in patients with COPD and risk factors for thromboembolism.
differential.trigger: Sudden onset dyspnea with pleuritic chest pain or unexplained hypoxemia.

history: Risk factors: recent surgery, immobilization, cancer, prior venous thromboembolism
exam: Clear lungs or focal crackles if pulmonary infarction
Signs of deep vein thrombosis: calf swelling or tenderness
labs: Arterial blood gas may show hypoxemia with widened A-a gradient
imaging: CT pulmonary angiography shows filling defect

differential.name: Bronchiectasis
differential.why_considered: Chronic cough with copious purulent sputum and recurrent infections overlaps with chronic bronchitis.

history: Recurrent pneumonia or chest infections since childhood
History of severe pneumonia, tuberculosis, or immunodeficiency
exam: Coarse crackles that persist and change location
labs: Sputum culture may show chronic Pseudomonas or other organisms
imaging: High-resolution CT shows dilated bronchi with signet ring sign
Chest X-ray may show tram-track lines

differential.name: Lung cancer
differential.why_considered: Chronic cough, weight loss, and hemoptysis in a smoker can overlap with COPD but require urgent evaluation.
differential.trigger: Hemoptysis or unintentional weight loss in a smoker with chronic cough.

exam: Focal decreased breath sounds or dullness if large mass
labs: May have anemia, hypercalcemia (squamous cell), or hyponatremia (small cell)
imaging: Chest CT shows lung mass or nodule
Chest X-ray may show opacity, atelectasis, or pleural effusion

differential.name: Tuberculosis
differential.why_considered: Chronic cough, fever, night sweats, and weight loss can mimic COPD exacerbations, especially in high-risk populations.

history: Chronic cough lasting more than 3 weeks
Exposure to someone with active tuberculosis
Risk factors: immigration from high-burden country, immunosuppression, incarceration
exam: Dullness to percussion if consolidation or effusion
labs: Sputum acid-fast bacilli smear and culture positive
Interferon-gamma release assay or tuberculin skin test positive
imaging: Chest X-ray shows upper lobe cavitary infiltrate or hilar adenopathy

differential.name: Interstitial lung disease
differential.why_considered: Progressive exertional dyspnea and dry cough with crackles can be mistaken for COPD.

history: Progressive exertional dyspnea over months to years
exam: Fine inspiratory crackles (Velcro) at lung bases
labs: May have positive autoimmune serologies (ANA, RF)
Pulmonary function tests show restrictive pattern with reduced DLCO
imaging: High-resolution CT shows reticular opacities, honeycombing, or ground-glass
Chest X-ray may show bilateral interstitial markings

severity.mild: Stable mild COPD: dyspnea on strenuous exertion, occasional cough, spirometry shows mild airflow obstruction (FEV1 ≥80% predicted after bronchodilator).
severity.moderate: Stable moderate COPD: dyspnea on moderate exertion, daily cough and sputum, spirometry shows moderate airflow obstruction (FEV1 50-79% predicted).
severity.severe: Stable severe COPD: dyspnea on minimal exertion, frequent exacerbations, spirometry shows severe airflow obstruction (FEV1 30-49% predicted), may have chronic hypoxemia or hypercapnia.
severity.critical: Acute exacerbation with acute respiratory failure: severe dyspnea at rest, use of accessory muscles, altered mental status, PaO2 <60 mmHg or PaCO2 >50 mmHg with acidemia, or requiring ventilatory support.

red_flags.finding: Oxygen saturation <88-90% (or <92% if acute) on room air
red_flags.meaning: Severe hypoxemia; high risk of respiratory failure

red_flags.finding: Inability to speak in full sentences or use of accessory muscles
red_flags.meaning: Severe airflow obstruction; impending respiratory failure

red_flags.finding: Respiratory rate >30 breaths/min or heart rate >120 beats/min

red_flags.meaning: Severe airflow obstruction with poor air movement; impending respiratory arrest

red_flags.finding: Acute respiratory acidosis (pH <7.35 with elevated PaCO2)

red_flags.meaning: Sepsis or tension pneumothorax (especially with unilateral absent breath sounds)

complications.name: Pneumonia
clues: New focal infiltrate on chest X-ray

special_populations.differences: More likely to have comorbid heart failure and may present with only fatigue or confusion during exacerbations; spirometry results must be interpreted with age-appropriate reference values; careful with polypharmacy and cognitive impairment.
Obesity hypoventilation syndrome often coexists; dyspnea may be attributed to obesity; assess for sleep-disordered breathing; spirometry may show a restrictive component.
Rare but high risk; physiologic changes worsen dyspnea; optimize oxygen and avoid contraindicated medications; multidisciplinary care with obstetrics.

key_questions.question: Have you ever smoked? How many pack-years?
key_questions.looking_for: Substantial cigarette smoking history, typically at least 10-20 pack-years

key_questions.question: When did the shortness of breath start, and how has it changed over time?
key_questions.looking_for: Progressive exertional dyspnea over months to years, not sudden onset

key_questions.question: Do you have a cough? How long have you had it?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic cough present for months to years

key_questions.question: Do you cough up phlegm? What color and how much?
key_questions.looking_for: Daily sputum production, often worse in the morning

key_questions.question: Have you been exposed to dust, fumes, or chemicals at work or home?
key_questions.looking_for: Occupational or environmental irritant exposures that contribute to COPD

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have COPD, emphysema, or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history, especially in younger or never-smoking patients, suggesting alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency

key_questions.question: Have you ever had asthma or other lung problems? Any frequent lung infections?
key_questions.looking_for: History of asthma or recurrent respiratory infections may coexist or predispose

key_questions.question: Have you had any chest pain, fever, or blood in your sputum?
key_questions.looking_for: Absence of these; presence suggests alternative diagnosis such as pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, or lung cancer

key_questions.question: Do you feel short of breath when lying flat? Any swelling in your legs?
key_questions.looking_for: Absence of orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or edema; presence suggests heart failure

reasoning_points: Substantial smoking history or other inhalational exposure
Chronic progressive dyspnea, cough, and sputum production over months to years
Physical exam findings of hyperinflation, decreased breath sounds, prolonged expiration, and wheezing
Spirometry confirms post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC less than 0.70, indicating persistent airflow obstruction
Chest X-ray showing hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms, or increased retrosternal air space supports the diagnosis
Minimal bronchodilator reversibility and smoking history help distinguish COPD from asthma
Severity assessed by GOLD criteria using FEV1 percent predicted and symptom/exacerbation burden
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency considered if atypical features such as young age, minimal smoking, or lower-lobe emphysema

easy: Older adult with a long smoking history
Classic progressive exertional dyspnea, chronic productive cough, and wheezing
Spirometry shows fixed airflow obstruction with post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC < 0.70
Chest X-ray reveals hyperinflation and flattened diaphragms
medium: Patient with coexisting heart failure, making dyspnea attribution challenging
Moderate COPD with some bronchodilator reversibility, raising question of asthma-COPD overlap
Younger patient with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and lower-lobe emphysema
Recent exacerbation with increased sputum purulence and dyspnea
hard: Never-smoker with only occupational or biomass fuel exposure
Severe emphysema with large bullae and risk of pneumothorax
Patient presenting with acute respiratory failure and altered mental status due to hypercapnia
Older patient with multiple comorbidities and unclear primary cause of dyspnea
